national.title: Nvidia stock slumps amid board investigation into CEO Jensen Huang
national.summary: Investors are questioning whether Huang's future as Nvidia's CEO may be at risk amid allegations that he was targeted in a Chinese intelligence operation.
national.body: Nvidia's stock price slid on Monday amid questions about CEO Jensen Huang's future at the chipmaker, following the board of directors' investigation into allegations that China targeted him in an intelligence operation.The investigation is raising concerns about Huang's role at the company, which he co-founded and helped build into the world's second-most valuable company, with a $4.5 trillion valuation. Nvidia is barred from selling its high-end chips, specifically designed to power artificial intelligence models, to China due to competitive concerns.Nvidia shares sank 4.7%, or $8.68, to $177.96 in late afternoon trading, shrinking the chipmaker's market valuation by about $211 billion.The allegations center around reports that Huang had a close relationship with Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence officials believe was a spy for China's Ministry of State Security, the country's main intelligence agency. On Sunday, Nvidia's board said it is starting an "independent investigation" into the allegations, sparking questions about the CEO's future with the company. "This is a black eye moment for Jensen and will spark multiple congressional inquiries at a minimum and will create an overhang on the stock for a myriad of reasons," Dan Ives, a tech analyst at Yorkville Ives, said in a research note. "The key question investors will be asking is: Will Jensen remain CEO of Nvidia?"Ives added, "There is clearly risk that Jensen could be removed as CEO depending on the board investigation, and this will add risk to the stock as he is so important to the Nvidia story and strategy globally."In a statement to CBS News, an Nvidia spokesperson said that "Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as CEO without interruption." The company didn't respond to a question about whether Huang had violated any of its corporate policies. The company's board said it had no reason to believe that the company's secrets or national security were compromised. John Rizzo, a spokesperson for Nvidia, told CBS News on Sunday, "We trust that if we were the target of a genuine threat, the U.S. government would have notified us."The Chinese government dismissed allegations that it targeted Nvidia's chief executive, who co-founded the company in 1993, as part of an espionage operation. national.summary: Rep. Thomas Massie moved Monday to force a vote to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, setting the stage for a dramatic vote on whether to remove one of the Trump administration's most prominent figures following sweeping election losses.
national.body:
Konstantin Toropin, Associated Press Konstantin Toropin, Associated Press

WASHINGTON (AP) — Rep. Thomas Massie moved Monday to force a vote to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, setting the stage for a dramatic vote on whether to remove one of the Trump administration's most prominent figures following sweeping election losses.

The impeachment resolution was introduced by Massie, a Kentucky Republican, as soon as the House opened for the first day of sessions after the midterms. It largely focuses on the war in Iran but also includes references to Hegseth's role in carrying out military actions in Yemen and Venezuela.

WATCH: Hegseth announces he will hold news conference on impeachment threat to defend his record

Massie said the secretary's actions amount to "high crimes and misdemeanors" and his leadership at the Pentagon "thus warrants impeachment."

A vote in the House could come by mid-week, putting pressure on Republicans — many of whom blamed their election wipeout on the Iran war — but next steps are highly uncertain.

House Speaker Mike Johnson had tried to prevent this outcome, and warned lawmakers against impeaching the Defense secretary while the U.S. is engaged in military actions in the Middle East.

national.title: Republican congressman to force impeachment vote on Defence Secretary Hegseth
national.summary: The effort will likely fail, but Representative Thomas Massie wants to push Trump to fire Hegseth before Democrats can launch their own impeachment process.
national.body:
A Republican congressman plans to force a vote in the House of Representatives this week to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, alleging he has violated the US Constitution.

"By engaging in hostilities in Iran for more than 90 days without congressional authorization, Secretary Hegseth is breaking the law and must be held accountable," Representative Thomas Massie said.

The effort will likely fail, given Republicans will remain in power in Congress until January. But Massie says he wants to push President Donald Trump to fire Hegseth before Democrats can launch their own impeachment process.

Hegseth, who will hold a news conference on Tuesday about Massie's move, said he was not concerned.

Massie formally introduced the articles of impeachment in a resolution on the House floor on Monday afternoon.

"We're not worried about that," Hegseth said when asked by reporters about the impending resolution earlier on Monday, adding he would hold a news conference Tuesday morning "on that very topic".

Massie, who lost re-election earlier this year, has been critical of Trump and the war in Iran since it started nearly nine months ago. He is known across the country for also pushing the administration to release federal files on the deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

The Kentucky congressman first introduced impeachment articles in September and is now pressing for a vote in the wake of Republicans losing control of both the House and Senate in last week's midterm elections. He has said his push to rid the administration of Hegseth is meant to prevent a Democrat spectacle next year.

national.title: France accuses Iran of supermarket fridge hacking
national.summary: Tons of chilled and frozen food was spoiled last month as fridges and freezers in hundreds of supermarkets heated up.
national.body:
France has accused Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) of being behind cyber-attacks that raised the temperatures of supermarket fridges and freezers across the country last month.

Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said the attack was "unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression", adding those who were responsible would be hit with sanctions.

Iran has yet to respond officially, but some Iranian media outlets have dismissed the allegations as baseless.

The French hacking, which led to the destruction of tons of frozen anc chilled food in France was followed by a similar attack against supermarkets across several other European countries. It is not known if the instances are linked.

Barrot said the attack on France's supermarkets "marks the first large-scale cyber-attack aimed at sabotage on our national territory, and it constitutes a major attack on the nation's interests and the security of the French people".

He said the government had summoned the Iranian ambassador to Paris to "lodge a very strong protest against this extremely grave act".

France will take "any other necessary and proportionate measures" to respond to the incident and "deter anyone who might seek to repeat it", Barrot added.

The Paris prosecutor said an investigation had been opened into the head of an offensive cyber unit associated with the IRGC as well as his two deputies.

national.summary: The share price dropped wiped hundreds of billions of dollars from the value of Nvidia.
national.body:
Hundreds of billions of dollars have been wiped off the value of Nvidia after the US chipmaker announced an independent investigation would be carried out into its chief executive's affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

The tech firm saw its shares fall by about 6% on Monday after Jensen Huang admitted having an extramarital affair.

Nvidia's probe came after reports that the US believed the Nvidia boss had been targeted in an espionage campaign by China.

However, China has rejected the claims, with its foreign ministry saying "allegations about Chinese spies were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China".

Nvidia said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised, but a statement by the firm's board of directors said it would begin an investigation in "light of recent reporting that founder and chief executive Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort".

US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report , external .

The report said Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington last spring warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.

Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia.

national.title: Even after the midterm rout of Trumpism, the world struggles to trust America
national.summary: The U.S. midterm rout of President Donald Trump's stewardship doesn't mean the world trusts America again.
national.body:
Laurie Kellman, Associated Press Laurie Kellman, Associated Press

LONDON (AP) — For Joe Reeve, the midterm afterglow faded fast.

The London startup founder was among the wave around the Trump-weary world awakening to the stunning news that Americans had sharply rejected President Donald Trump's fist-in-the-eye stewardship of the United States that had started a war with Iran, forged no peace in Ukraine or the Mideast and made gas and food so expensive.

Voters, Reeve saw online, had flipped control of both houses of Congress, handing the power to check the president to his rival Democrats. American democracy, 250 years on, had survived the Trump era.

But a deep and profound distrust of the United States had survived the vote, too. And from national leaders to aspiring American immigrants, no one seemed confident that change was afoot.

"What everybody's learned," Reeve, 29, the husband of a Ukrainian, said a day later in an interview, "is that America's system does allow for these wild swings. We all know, now, that America has an ability to rotate on a dime and spit in our faces."

Interviews by The Associated Press around the world since the vote revealed a sense that "one election alone does not restore anything," as Kim So-jung, 49, an office worker in Yongin, South Korea, put it. "We have to see what they actually do, and see that they are doing something different to gain at least a little trust back."

That 77 million Americans voted to elect Trump to a second term, along with the administration's combative conduct on his tariff war, Israel's conduct in Gaza, immigration and Iran, had already shaken trust in America around the world.

national.title: U.S. gas prices on track to fall below $4 a gallon, experts say
national.summary: Fuel prices have dropped in recent weeks amid hopes that the midterm elections would increase pressure on the U.S. and Iran to reach a peace deal.
national.body: Motorists could soon see U.S. gasoline prices fall below $4 a gallon for the first time since July, according to energy experts.Patrick De Haan, a petroleum expert at price-tracking firm GasBuddy, told CBS News that he expects the national average for gas, which the price-tracking firm put at $4.06 a gallon on Thursday, to dip below the $4 threshold by next week. He also predicted diesel could fall below $6 a gallon by Thanksgiving.The average price was still at $4.06 early Friday, according to GasBuddy.Gas and diesel prices have both dropped in recent weeks. The decline was partially due to market expectations that the U.S. midterm elections would underscore public dissatisfaction with the war in Iran and increase pressure on the Trump administration to strike a deal ending the conflict, De Haan said."Oil prices have been falling in the run-up to the election," he said. "My read is because there was optimism that after the midterms these problems would be addressed."Other factors pushing down gas pricesOther factors are also putting downward pressure on fuel costs. Oil tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has picked up, easing constraints on global oil supply, De Haan said. Brent crude, the international benchmark, fell below $100 on Thursday for the first time since September, trading at $97.44 by midday. West Texas Intermediate, the U.S. benchmark, was trading at $90.42 a barrel.The recent drop in gas prices is also partly due to seasonal shifts. Prices tend to dip in the fall when Americans pull back on road trips and summer travel, De Haan noted. Filling stations are already switching to winter-blend gas, which is less costly to produce than summer-blend fuel.Tom Kloza, chief energy adviser for Gulf Oil, predicts that the average U.S. gas price will sink below $4 within the next 10 days. The profit gas stations earn on each gallon of gas sold — currently around 75 cents per gallon — is also larger than usual."Historically, that is too outsized," he said in an email. national.title: In memoir, Biden says Trump should carry the weight of Jan. 6 riots 'to his grave'
national.summary: The first excerpt of "Promise Me, America" was published Monday by The Atlantic. The full memoir is set for a Nov. 17 release.
national.body:
ATLANTA (AP) — Former U.S. President Joe Biden writes in his White House memoir that Donald Trump, at once his predecessor and successor, has deeply damaged the country and world with an administration determined to "tear down institutions and inflame hatreds."

And the 83-year-old Democrat said the 80-year-old Trump's years of lies about his 2020 defeat to Biden and the Jan. 6 attacks on the Capitol should "follow him to his grave."

Biden's sweeping indictment comes in the first excerpt of "Promise Me, America," published Monday by The Atlantic. The 46th president's full memoir is set for a Nov. 17 release. Biden said that while doctors are encouraged by his response to cancer treatment, his activities promoting the book will be limited because of his health.

"Donald Trump led an insurrection," Biden wrote of the attack by Trump supporters as the U.S. Congress met to certify the 2020 election won by the Democrat. "His goal was to remain in power after the American people had voted him out of office.

"The rioters weren't 'peaceful protesters," he wrote. "They came armed to stop the official certification of a legitimate election." He chided Trump for later issuing more than 1,500 pardons of the offenders.

"To this day, Trump and his supporters continue to preen and posture like they're supporters of law enforcement," Biden wrote. "Here's my view: You don't get to turn a blind eye to cops being punched, speared, sprayed, and brutalized and call yourself a friend of law enforcement. What Trump did on January 6, 2021, should never be forgotten. It should follow him to his grave."

FILE PHOTO: A man breaks a window as a mob of supporters of U.S. President Donald Trump storm the U.S. Capitol Building in Washington, U.S., January 6, 2021. Photo by Leah Millis/Reuters.

Biden also laments Trump's Department of Government Efficiency and his aggressive reversal of many of his policies, especially those intended to address climate change.

national.title: Democrats plan to challenge Trump's fossil fuel agenda and push clean energy to lower bills
national.summary: Some Democrats are promising to push for more clean energy to help tackle rising energy costs when they take control of Congress in January, though President Donald Trump says he will use his veto power aggressively.
national.body:
Jennifer McDermott, Associated Press Jennifer McDermott, Associated Press

Some Democrats are promising to push for more clean energy to help tackle rising energy costs when they take control of Congress in January, though President Donald Trump says he will use his veto power aggressively.

With new majorities in the House and Senate after last week's midterms, Democrats can set an agenda boosting clean energy and addressing climate change. While those are traditionally core priorities of the party, climate was not a central topic in this election cycle.

Democrats can begin investigations and hold hearings into climate policy rollbacks and elimination of green energy grants by the Republican administration, potentially trying to undo some changes and restore renewable energy incentives.

Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, the top Democrat on the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works, said Trump's clean energy attacks drove up prices for taxpayers. He said Democrats will "work every angle to lower consumers' energy costs, and we will demand accountability for the massive corruption wrought by Trump's fossil-fuel donors."

American Clean Power Association CEO Jason Grumet said everybody who is trying to build clean energy "feels bolstered."

Enacting major changes would require Republican support because Democrats will lack the numbers to override presidential vetoes. Even then, lower energy bills are not guaranteed because prices also depend on fuel costs, demand and the expense of maintaining the electric grid.

"The wins give Democrats more leverage over spending and more political power to advance a coherent agenda; the question is whether they'll use that power effectively," said Lisa Sachs, director of the Columbia Center on Sustainable Investment. "The vote was for affordability and opportunity. Democrats now need to be clear about which policies deliver them."

national.title: These House and Senate midterm races don't have winners yet
national.summary: Democrats won sizable House and Senate majorities in the 2026 midterm elections, but the exact margins are unclear because some races haven't been projected yet. Here's where the results stand.
national.body: Washington — The makeup of Congress shifted dramatically in the 2026 midterm elections, as Democrats decisively won control of the Senate and picked up dozens of House seats — in what's on track to be one of the largest midterm routs in recent decades.The exact margins of Congress are not yet clear, as winners have not yet been projected in two Senate races and more than two dozen House races. They include GOP-held districts with razor-thin margins, a few Democratic seats that could flip to Republicans and several races in California and other Western states that still need to count ballots.Here's a look at the congressional races that CBS News has not yet projected, including where the results stand:Senate Toss-UpsDemocrats are set to enter next year with at least 54 Senate seats, compared to Republicans' 44. Two Senate races still haven't been called — one has long been viewed as a battleground, and the other came out of nowhere.Alaska Senate: Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan is running for reelection against Democrat Mary Peltola, a razor-thin race rocked by a last-minute scandal over how another Dan Sullivan got on the ballot. The count could drag on due to both outstanding ballots and Alaska's ranked choice voting system, which allows voters to rank candidates in order of preference. If no candidate is the top choice of a majority of voters, the last-place candidate is eliminated and the counting process moves to a second round. Final results aren't expected until 15 days after Election Day. Both the Sullivan and Peltola campaigns have argued they have the upper hand.Mississippi Senate: The race between GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and Democrat Scott Colom was not widely expected to be competitive, but it remains a toss-up. State officials say thousands of mail ballots are outstanding and can legally arrive within five days of the election, and there are an unknown number of "affidavit" ballots from voters whose eligibility needs to be checked. Colom and Hyde-Smith have both predicted that they'll emerge victorious.Democrats on DefenseThe dozens of red districts that Democrats flipped were the primary story of Tuesday night, but a few Republican House candidates are still trying to swim against the tide, either due to redistricting or a favorable local political makeup.Maine's 2nd District: This red, pro-Trump district is one of Republicans' top opportunities

WASHINGTON (AP) — The Senate on Monday is set to take up bipartisan legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews for data centers and other infrastructure projects, in the first major action since last week's election that soundly repudiated President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans.

The Senate is expected to hold a procedural vote on the bill, which senators and the president have pushed as officials seek to meet growing demand for electricity and other forms of energy that now faces yearslong delays in getting to the grid.

The legislation's sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to get big energy projects started — both for clean energy and fossil fuel projects — and make sure data centers pay for the energy they use. Anger over artificial intelligence data centers and rising electricity helped usher in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the massive, energy-hungry structures.

national.title: COP31 climate summit begins after disastrous year of extreme weather
national.summary: orld leaders, delegates and climate activists on Monday kicked off talks in Turkey on curbing climate change, which in the last year has led to rising temperatures and deadly heat waves in Europe and beyond.
national.body:
Suzan Fraser, Associated Press Suzan Fraser, Associated Press

ANTALYA, Turkey (AP) — World leaders, delegates and climate activists on Monday kicked off talks in Turkey on curbing climate change, which in the last year has led to rising temperatures and deadly heat waves in Europe and beyond, and played a role in disasters such as the devastating floods in Nepal.

This U.N. climate summit — called the Conference of the Parties, or COP31 — comes as the war in Iran has effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, hiking global prices of gasoline, oil and products made with them, such as fertilizers and pesticides. The disruption has pushed governments to rethink energy policies and increased investment in renewable energy sources like wind and solar.

"For too many people, climate change is deadly," U.N. climate chief Simon Stiell said on Monday. "At this COP, nations face a choice: electric or shock. Rewire the global economy for the electric age. Or accept ongoing fossil fuel cost pain for families, firms and governments."

"The climate crisis is now a global health crisis of pandemic proportions," he said.

Earlier, Stiell also said that agreeing on practical solutions, such as reducing methane emissions, can be "planetary icepacks" that can help reduce global heating. Methane stays in the atmosphere for a shorter time but warms the planet much faster than other planet-heating gases. Using renewable-powered electricity instead of oil, gas and coal can also help reduce global warming.

Delegates, meeting in the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya, will come under pressure to develop new pledges for climate action while implementing previous promises. The stakes are high: Climate scientists say global warming is likely to exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above the preindustrial levels of the early 1800s.

Limiting temperature rise to that threshold was a goal established during the 2015 Paris Agreement. Since then, it's been a focus of international climate negotiations.

national.title: Outdated power grids a major hurdle in renewable energy transition
national.summary: Outdated power grids around the world are a major hurdle in the transition from fossil fuels to renewable energy. Older grids often can't absorb all the electricity generated by new solar and wind installations.
national.body:
Anton L. Delgado, Associated Press Anton L. Delgado, Associated Press

Outdated power grids are a major hurdle in the transition to renewable energy, since older systems often can't absorb all the electricity from new, cleaner sources.

This threatens global efforts to curb climate change by reducing fossil fuels and switching to renewable energy such as solar and wind. At U.N. climate talks kicking off this week, co-hosts Turkey and Australia want more ambitious goals to slash fossil fuels, install renewables and upgrade grids.

Grid concerns are gaining urgency this year as nations race to improve their energy security following the Iran war. The U.N. recently launched a new initiative to rally funding for grid upgrades in Africa and Southeast Asia.

"There needs to be a massive, massive, massive scaling up of investments into grids if we are going to get close to meeting our climate, energy and development goals," Selwin Hart, special adviser to the U.N. secretary-general on climate action, said.

At the U.N. climate talks, hosted in the Turkish resort city of Antalya, organizers describe modern and reliable electric grids as "the backbone of the clean energy system."

But billions of dollars are needed to upgrade out-of-date grids. These steep costs could hinder further renewable energy installations.

During the U.N. General Assembly in September, the global body launched a Global Grids Accelerator to speed up international funding for electricity infrastructure in Africa and Southeast Asia.

Russia's leading independent newspaper closes after eviction Close Russia's leading independent newspaper has closed after being evicted from its offices and facing pressure from authorities.

For 30 years, Novaya Gazeta published investigations into corruption, human rights violations and abuse of power in the country.

On Monday, the team behind the newspaper had a final editorial meeting before packing up their belongings and leaving.

The Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia's media was highly diverse and that the newspaper's closure was part of "a standard rotational process".

The BBC spoke to its co-founder Dmitry Muratov, a Nobel Peace Prize winner, about the closure.

national.title: Turkey steel factory blast kills at least 16 people
national.summary: Eyewitnesses say the explosion shook the ground, with one believing an earthquake had hit near the Habas Demir Celik plant in Aliaga.
national.body:
At least 16 people have died and 13 others have been injured in an explosion at an iron and steel factory near the port city of Izmir in western Turkey.

All those killed and injured were workers at the Habas plant, one of the country's leading steel producers, authorities said. Footage from the scene showed a large fire inside the facility and a towering column of smoke rising into the air.

The local governor said the blast happened around midday after a crane carrying a replacement boiler collapsed, causing materials to fall into a furnace below.

Workplace accidents remain a chronic problem in Turkey, the Turkish Health and Safety Labor Watch, an independent civil society organisation, said.

Eyewitnesses said the explosion shook the ground, with one person initially believing an earthquake had struck.

In a statement, the company said the accident occurred during scheduled maintenance work on one of the plant's electric arc furnaces.

Izmir Governor Süleyman Elban told media that some people are believed to be still under the rubble.

Speaking after a cabinet meeting on Monday, Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan confirmed the deaths and said investigations were under way, while search and rescue operations continued. He also said two of the injured were in a serious condition.

national.title: Trump questions midterm elections integrity after previously accepting results
national.summary: Trump made the claims, without evidence, on Truth Social on Monday.
national.body:
US President Donald Trump has questioned the legitimacy of the midterm election results in which Republicans suffered sweeping losses, days after saying he would accept the outcome.

"Does anybody really believe that this 'Election' was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong?" Trump wrote on Truth Social on Monday.

This appeared to contradict what he told the New York Times on election night that he was "absolutely willing" to accept the results.

Democrats retook both chambers of Congress in last week's elections. State and local officials across the US said voting had been mostly problem-free.

Some key races, including Senate contests in Alaska and Mississippi, have yet to be called.

Trump says US voter fraud is 'rampant' - evidence suggests it is extremely rare

Published 27 October In the Truth Social post, Trump made vague claims about polling, voting "dumps", and "machines" without providing specific evidence of what this referred to and whether he believed there had been error or wrongdoing.

The reporting of vote counts on election night proceeded as normal, according to Charles Stewart III, a political scientist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT).

national.title: Russia-Ukraine peace talks led by U.S. will look at security guarantees for both sides
national.summary: The negotiations follow last month's localized truce around the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in southern Ukraine that allowed the evacuation of some trapped residents and the delivery of desperately needed humanitarian supplies.
national.body:
For the first time since February, Russian, Ukrainian and U.S. negotiators are scheduled to hold talks on ending the full-scale war that is nearing the five-year mark, with security guarantees topping the agenda.

The two-day session starting Tuesday in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, follows previous negotiations early this year that failed to produce any visible progress toward ending Europe's most devastating conflict since World War II.

The talks follow last month's localized truce around the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in southern Ukraine that was brokered with the help of U.S. first lady Melania Trump and allowed the evacuation of some of its residents and the delivery of desperately needed humanitarian supplies.

But even as Moscow and Kyiv touted the weeklong ceasefire as a positive model, fierce fighting has continued along the 1,200-kilometer (750-mile) front line. Both sides also have escalated their long-range attacks on each other with drones and missiles.

Russia has intensified its strikes on Ukraine's power system, seeking to undermine the country's resolve as winter sets in. Moscow has relied on ballistic missiles and new, faster jet-powered drones, taking advantage of Ukraine's shortage of U.S.-made Patriot interceptors.

Russia and Ukraine remain far apart on key elements of any prospective peace deal.

Russian President Vladimir Putin wants Ukraine to pull its troops back from the four regions that Moscow illegally annexed in September 2022 but never fully captured. He also demands that Ukraine abandon its bid to join NATO, accept strict limits on its military and drop restrictions on the Russian language and the Moscow-affiliated Orthodox Church in Ukraine.

Putin wants a comprehensive peace deal on those conditions and won't agree to a general halt in hostilities, arguing such a pause would only allow Ukrainian troops to rest and replenish their weapons stockpiles.

national.title: Russia and Ukraine exchange strikes a day before U.S.-brokered talks are scheduled to begin
national.summary: President Donald Trump mentioned in a "60 Minutes" interview that the two sides are "very close" to a deal.
national.body:
KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Russia battered Ukraine's power grid again and Ukrainian forces hit another of Russia's biggest oil refineries, officials said Monday, hours before delegations from Moscow and Kyiv were due to meet for new U.S.-brokered talks on how to end the fighting.

Nearly five years after Russia invaded its neighbor, the two countries remain locked in battle with no sign that either side is ready to budge from their demands. The war has already killed hundreds of thousands of soldiers and thousands of civilians, analysts and humanitarian organizations say.

The three-way talks between envoys from the U.S., Russia and Ukraine are due to start in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, on Tuesday and last for two days. The previous round of talks was in February.

U.S. President Donald Trump said in a "60 Minutes" interview that aired Sunday that Moscow and Kyiv are "very close" to a deal, despite the "tremendous hatred" between Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

He said that Ukraine would have "a little bit different shape" under the settlement, but he didn't elaborate.

Trump has previously made statements about developments in the war which haven't materialized.

Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, who will mediate in the talks with U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff, said that the priorities will be ending the conflict, finding ways to stop the war reigniting, reviving Ukraine's postwar economy and preparing humanitarian aid.

"We hope these discussions will identify areas of common ground, advance practical solutions, and build momentum toward the next phase of negotiations," Kushner said on X Monday.

national.title: Nine Zimbabweans caught allegedly trying to leave South Africa to fight in Ukraine
national.summary: Hundreds of people from different African countries have been recruited to fight for Russia, according to Ukraine.
national.body:
Nine Zimbabweans have been arrested in South Africa after they were caught allegedly trying to leave the country to fight in the war between Russia and the Ukraine, police say.

The group, aged between 20 and 26, were arrested in and around Johannesburg by a multidisciplinary team on Sunday evening.

They were caught as they were "preparing to board flights out of the country", authorities added, but their final destination is unclear.

They have been charged with contravening South Africa's Regulation of Foreign Military Assistance Act, which outlaws mercenary activity without government permission.

Police said five people were arrested at South Africa's biggest airport, OR Tambo, and another four at a hotel in Bruma, east of Johannesburg by a multidisciplinary team that involved Interpol.

All nine later appeared in court, according to state prosecutors.

The police statement added that the involvement of Interpol and other international law enforcement agencies indicated that the suspects had also allegedly violated laws in their respective home countries, prompting cooperation with South African authorities.

They have also not said whether the group allegedly intended to fight for Russia or Ukraine nor provided details of the organisations allegedly involved in facilitating their travel.

national.title: Watch: Rare insight into France's drug gangs recruiting children to commit violence
national.summary: "It destroys people, but we all make our own choices" - Marseille drug-gang members spoke to the BBC.
national.body:
Watch: Rare insight into France's drug gangs recruiting children to commit violence Close A BBC investigation has found one of Europe's most powerful drug gangs in France is recruiting teenage children from across the country to commit kidnap and murder.

Known as the "DZ Mafia", the gang won a bloody turf war against a rival group in Marseille during 2023, and is now recruiting from further afield.

One member who is in prison awaiting trial after being implicated in several murders told the BBC he was part of a DZ Mafia hit squad.

He agrees the killings he has been charged with were "quite shocking".

"Attempts in broad daylight, in traffic jams… it can range from going to hit a guy, slap him to taking him in front of his mother and burning him up in a car. I think I have good composure, I handle it fairly well."

When challenged over whether he feels regret when carrying out such acts of brutality, he says he feels "guilty in-part" but claims to have no regrets.

Like so many teenagers from Marseille, he knew large sums of money could be earned quickly in drug trafficking. Now in his twenties, he admits the environment he entered was a "trap".

The BBC's Paris Correspondent, James Waterhouse, reports from Marseille.

national.title: Russell Brand is sentenced to more than 10 years in prison for rape and sexual assault
national.summary: A jury found him guilty of attacking four of six accusers, with allegations dating back to 2004.
national.body:
Brian Melley, Associated Press Brian Melley, Associated Press

Editor's Note: This story contains descriptions of sexual assault.

LONDON (AP) — Russell Brand was sentenced Monday to 10½ years in prison for raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others at a time when his bawdy behavior was indulged and celebrated during his rise to stardom.

Judge Joel Bennathan denounced Brand's "casual and arrogant disregard" for any woman who said no to him, and castigated him for the series of lies he told in testimony denying assaults that dated back to 2004.

"About 20 years ago, Russell Brand, you were becoming famous," Bennathan said. "You were clever — and in many people's eyes, funny and charismatic. You had also become a sexual predator."

Brand showed little emotion during the stinging rebuke. He turned to mouth the words "we'll be OK" to his wife after he stood up and was led away by court officers after the hearing.

The 51-year-old actor-comedian, known for outrageous stand-up routines and provocative behavior on television and radio broadcasts, as well as battles with drugs and alcohol, had maintained his innocence and testified that all his encounters were consensual.

But a jury of eight men and four women found him guilty of attacking four of six accusers. He was cleared of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.

national.title: Razor-tight Mississippi Senate race sparks ballot battle - could there be a recount?
national.summary: Lawyers for both campaigns in Mississippi's US Senate race are preparing for a possible legal battle as the close count continues.
national.body:
The Democrats hold a narrow lead over the Republicans in the US Senate race in Mississippi, with both sides in a dispute over the counting of the remaining votes which could decide the outcome.

Lawyers for each campaign are preparing for a possible legal battle over the final results and weighing in on the examination of ballots.

The result could mark the end of almost 40 years of Republican control over Mississippi's senate seats and will determine the size of the Democrats' majority in the upper house.

Mississippi is the only US state which does not have a set procedure in place to trigger a recount - and the pressure is on to declare a winner with the state's 13 November deadline for certification approaching.

With 97% of the votes counted as of Monday, Democratic candidate Scott Colom is about 2,500 votes ahead of the incumbent Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith.

Mississippi's Secretary of State Michael Watson said on Sunday that about 2,700 absentee mail-in ballots were still to be counted. The state can accept these votes so long as they were postmarked by election day and are received by 10 November.

Watson also said more than 14,000 affidavit ballots, also known as provisional ballots, had been processed. These are typically cast when a voter lacked the required identification to cast their vote. The deadline for voters to resolve any ID issues with provisional ballots, usually by providing acceptable photo identification, is also 10 November.

It's unclear how many of these still need to be counted. Mississippi's Republican Party Chair Michael Hurst told CNN on Friday , external that they estimated there could be up to 25,000 affidavit ballots remaining.

national.title: At least 39 die after Europe-bound migrant boat sinks off Senegal
national.summary: The Atlantic crossing to Spain's Canary Islands remains dangerous for migrants seeking a better life
national.body:
At least 39 people have died after a boat carrying migrants sank off the coast of Senegal, the Senegalese Press Agency (APS) reports.

The interior ministry said one person had been rescued, but the number of people still missing was yet to be established.

The small wooden boat capsized between the capital, Dakar and the northern city of Saint-Louis, as it headed towards Spain's Canary Islands.

Spanish migrant rights group Walking Borders recorded 635 deaths on the Atlantic route to the Canary Islands between January and May 2026, the highest toll among the routes it monitors.

Saliou Diouf, founder of Senegalese migrant aid group Boza Fii, told the AFP news agency that all the bodies recovered by Sunday evening were Senegalese. The nationalities of other people on board was yet to be established, as search operations continued.

Four bodies were recovered on Monday morning in an advanced state of decomposition and buried following a collective funeral prayer organised by the fire service.

Rescue teams are searching along a 25km (15-mile)- stretch of coastline, but operations have been complicated by difficult access and strong ocean currents, which are pushing bodies further south.

Authorities say 24 of the 39 victims have been identified and their bodies returned to their families, while 11 others are still awaiting identification.

national.title: Trump says idea to make UFC's Dana White his press secretary 'just a little fun'
national.summary: Trump does not currently have a press secretary after briefly giving the job to Katie Zacharia, who left the post after five days.
national.body:
Michelle L. Price, Associated Press Michelle L. Price, Associated Press

WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. (AP) — President Donald Trump said Sunday he was only kidding about making UFC boss Dana White his next White House press secretary after announcing on social media he had offered his close friend the job.

After his party's deep losses in Tuesday's midterm elections, Trump shook up his administration on Friday by replacing his chief of staff and followed up on Saturday with a post that said he had offered the press secretary job to White. On Sunday, Trump said it was "just a little fun."

"I was kidding, but I think Dana likes the idea, and he is a very capable guy," Trump said, speaking to reporters in Florida before departing for the White House. White is set to visit him at the White House on Monday.

The historic wins by Democratic candidates, including in areas that Republicans had held for decades, led to the GOP losing control of both chambers of Congress.

Trump on Friday named longtime aide Stephen Miller as his new chief of staff , replacing Susie Wiles. Miller is the architect of the administration's hardline immigration policies. Trump does not currently have a press secretary after briefly giving the job to Katie Zacharia , who faltered behind the lectern and in interviews, and left the post after five days.

The House and Senate are in session for just six short weeks of a lame-duck sprint to finish up the Republican agenda before the the change of power on Jan. 3, 2027.

Leadership elections and a government funding package are all priorities ahead. But a first order of business is expected to be a resolution to impeach Hegseth.

It's unclear if Johnson will be able to slow the impeachment drive now, unless he decides to adjourn the chamber again.

national.title: Trump says his deportation policy 'might have been too tough' for midterm voters
national.summary: Trump said that he thinks he can work with Democrats in the new Congress on some kind of immigration deal.
national.body:
Mike Catalini, Associated Press Mike Catalini, Associated Press

Darlene Superville, Associated Press Darlene Superville, Associated Press

President Donald Trump, in his first major interview since his party lost control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections, said he thinks his administration was too aggressive on deportations and that he thinks he can work with Democrats in the new Congress on some kind of immigration deal.

Trump said his deportation policy was part of the reason Republicans lost, telling CBS's "60 Minutes" in an interview that aired on Sunday: "I think it might be too tough, yeah."

He added that he thinks he could reach an agreement with the new Democratic majority . "The deal would be we would work something out. And I think it's something -- I think that's something that's actually doable," he said in the interview.

Trump did not give specifics about what that deal would look like — and shortly after taping the interview on Friday, Trump named the key architect of his hard-line immigration agenda, Stephen Miller, as his new chief of staff.

"Trump says his immigration crackdown went too far," Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer scoffed on social media Sunday after the interview aired. "Apparently, his solution was to put the man responsible for it in charge of the White House. That's not a course correction. That's a promotion."

The president's immigration crackdown was a prominent feature of his return to office with major operations in multiple cities sending arrests soaring. Two U.S. citizens — Renee Good and Alex Pretti — were killed by federal officers during protests against the operations.

national.summary: The billionaire tech executive finds himself mired in a personal and national security scandal.
national.body:
One of the Artificial Intelligence (AI) industry's most important figures has been accused of having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, prompting an investigation.

US intelligence officials believed that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who had a close relationship with Nvidia CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang, was a spy for Beijing , according to a New York Times report.

On Sunday, Huang admitted , external to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children.

US tech giant Nvidia, one of the most valuable companies in the world, has opened an independent investigation into the reports. The firm said it does not believe US national security had been compromised - and added that Huang was committed to continuing to lead the company.

national.title: Thick smog shrouds New Delhi after Diwali firecrackers add to seasonal pollution
national.summary: New Delhi, home to over 30 million people, regularly ranks among the world's most polluted areas during winter, with pollution worsening in late October and November.
national.body:
People walk in front of India Gate, shrouded in thick smog after firecrackers lit up the sky overnight during Diwali celebrations, in New Delhi, Monday, Nov. 9, 2026. Manish Swarup/AP hide caption

NEW DELHI — A thick blanket of smog shrouded India's capital Monday after firecrackers lit up the skies over New Delhi during Diwali celebrations, compounding dangerously high pollution levels and intensifying the seasonal air pollution crisis that grips the city every year.

Despite restrictions on fireworks, residents in New Delhi celebrated the Hindu festival of lights with firecrackers on Sunday evening, releasing smoke and fine particulate matter into the atmosphere. The air quality index exceeded 350 in several parts of the capital on Monday morning, reaching the severe category and posing significant health risks.

Monitoring stations across the city recorded similarly alarming levels, while visibility deteriorated as a gray haze blanketed streets and high-rise buildings.

India's Supreme Court in October had sought to limit Diwali pollution by restricting conventional firecrackers and allowing only approved "green firecrackers" under specified conditions for three-hour windows on Saturday and Sunday. The crackers produce fewer emissions but are not pollution-free. They still release particulate matter and other pollutants, adding to the city's already hazardous air.

Isyad, a New Delhi resident who uses one name, said the worsening smog was taking a toll on his health.

"Because of the pollution there is irritation in the throat and itching in the eyes," he said.

New Delhi and its metropolitan region, home to more than 30 million people, regularly rank among the world's most polluted areas during winter. Pollution worsens as Diwali fireworks coincide with cooler weather and smoke from crop-residue fires in neighboring states of Punjab and Haryana.

national.title: Deportation flight of Iranians from U.S. canceled at last minute, attorney says
national.summary: The U.S. Department of Homeland Security refused to comment on the details of removal operations.
national.body:
Safiyah Riddle, Associated Press Safiyah Riddle, Associated Press

LOS ANGELES (AP) — A U.S. deportation flight of Iranian nationals bound for Iran by way of Pakistan was abruptly canceled Sunday morning, according to an attorney who spoke to some of the detainees slated for repatriation.

At least eight Iranians were loaded onto a plane Sunday morning in Mesa, Arizona, for a deportation flight headed to the country of Georgia, then on to Pakistan, according to Ali Rahnama, an attorney with the Iranian American Legal Defense Fund who filed emergency motions on behalf of some of the Iranian detainees. The flight was canceled without explanation, he said.

Court documents unsealed days ago in a civil lawsuit filed by the fund showed the Trump administration as recently as mid-October said it had plans to deport the Iranians to Iran, even as the war there drags on, via an unnamed third country. The lawsuit was filed in July and alleges that the U.S. government illegally shared confidential information about Iranians seeking asylum in the U.S. with Iranian officials.

There were three deportation flights to Iran between September 2025 and January 2026, with over 100 Iranian nationals deported. But the administration's confirmation of the new plans amid the war that began in February highlights its resolve in carrying out its hardline immigration crackdown, which has involved ramping up removals, including to places that critics say could endanger the lives of the returnees.

In response to questions Sunday from The Associated Press, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that Immigration and Customs Enforcement does not comment on "prospective removal operations, including flight schedules, passenger manifests, destinations, or individual case details," nor would the agency confirm future removal operations.

"As promised, the Trump Administration is employing all lawful options to carry out the largest deportation operation in history," the statement said.

The administration did not specify in the October court records when the deportations would be carried out. But in the past week, roughly a dozen Iranian nationals in immigration detention said they were notified that they were scheduled for an upcoming deportation flight to Pakistan and then to Iran, according to numerous attorneys who have since confirmed those plans with DHS.

national.title: Pope visits care home in Argentina for people with disabilities, renewing call to protect the vulnerable
national.summary: Known as the "city of charity," it has been hit hard by President Javier Milei's austerity measures, which have severely affected healthcare and social services.
national.body:
Nicole Winfield, Associated Press Nicole Winfield, Associated Press

Almudena Calatrava, Associated Press Almudena Calatrava, Associated Press

BUENOS AIRES, Argentina (AP) — Pope Leo XIV renewed his call Monday for Argentina to protect its weakest and most vulnerable people as he visited a home for people with disabilities in a symbolically powerful rebuke of President Javier Milei's austerity measures.

On his first full day in Argentina, Leo made a pilgrimage to the Cottolengo Don Orione in Claypole, south of Buenos Aires. Founded by an Italian priest in 1935, the institution houses more than 400 people with disabilities on its 123-acre (50-hectare) grounds.

The center, known as the "city of charity," has been hit hard by Milei's austerity measures, which have severely affected healthcare and social services. Milei has taken his signature chain saw to specialized therapy programs that for decades have been a lifeline for many of Argentina's estimated 5 million people with disabilities, freezing payments and dismantling a vital safety net.

Some residents and employees wept as Leo arrived Monday and embraced people in wheelchairs. He chatted with them and blessed them and told them their lives were a blessing, not a burden on society.

"You can help us to remember the foundation of the dignity of every human being and what is truly important in life," Leo said in the center's chapel. He said he dreamed that Argentines would be inspired to replace the pursuit of economic success and the "cult of outward appearances" with "great works of charity" like the Cottolengo home.

"A nation's progress is also measured by how it welcomes all people with disabilities and particular needs," he said.

national.title: British comedian Russell Brand sentenced to over 10 years for rape and sexual assault
national.summary: Russell Brand, who became a celebrity darling in the early 2000s, was found guilty on one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault in a case brought by six women.
national.body:
This is a court artist sketch by Elizabeth Cook of Russell Brand in the dock at Southwark Crown Court, in London, on Nov. 5. Elizabeth Cook/PA/AP hide caption

Russell Brand, the raunchy, irreverent British comedian who became a celebrity darling in the early 2000s, has been sentenced to over 10 years in prison after being found guilty on one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

"The total sentence is one of ten years, six months," said Judge Justice Bennathan on handing down the sentence at Southwark Crown Court in London on Monday.

Brand, 51, was a career chameleon who went from stand-up comic and MTV host to a political analyst esteemed by Britain's left, only to become a conspiracy theorist and Christian convert beloved by the U.S. right.

But critics of Brand said there was always a clear thread of misogyny running through his comedy routines, and that his mistreatment of women had been an open secret for decades.

Over the past four weeks, six women testified against the comedian in court in London, in a trial that garnered massive media attention.

A jury found Brand guilty last week on four of the seven counts against him. He was found guilty of raping a woman he'd met at one of his shows in 2009 and of sexually assaulting three women — at a bar, a radio station and a TV studio — between 2004 and 2009.

Brand denies all charges and said he never had non-consensual sex.

national.title: Musk says Tesla will return some Cybertruck deposits
national.summary: Musk said Monday that the Cybertruck order rate "far exceeds" Tesla's production pace.
national.body: Elon Musk said Monday that Tesla will return Cybertruck deposits to some of its customers as the company prepares to wind down production of the electric pickup truck.In announcing the decision in a Monday social media post, Musk said that the Cybertruck order rate "far exceeds" Tesla's production rate."We will try to make as many as possible before shutting down the line in about 8 months, but will have to return deposits for a lot of people," the Tesla CEO wrote.Musk announced last week that Tesla would stop producing the Cybertruck at its Texas factory by mid-2027 to "make room for increased Cybercab production," referring to the company's robotaxi line.Wall Street analyst Dan Ives, who is the senior managing director of Yorkville Ives & Co., told CBS News the "writing was on the wall" given the Cybertruck's high price and low demand. Ending production will free up time for Musk to focus on robotics and robotaxis, he added.In his Monday post, Musk disputed claims that Tesla was ending production of the Cybertruck because it was unprofitable. Rather, he said, the "opportunity cost of the complexity of Cybertruck is vastly outweighed by the value of incremental Cybercab production."Tesla launched the Cybertruck in 2019 for a starting price of $69,000.In an X post Saturday, Musk said Tesla would continue Cybertruck production for another eight to nine months before shifting focus to scaling the Cybercab. "There will never be another vehicle like it," he said of the Cybertruck.

national.title: Thirteen migrants die after boat sinks off Crete
national.summary: The Greek coastguard says it has rescued 18 people, all of whom were Sudanese nationals.
national.body:
At least 13 people have died after a boat carrying migrants sank off the coast of the Greek island of Crete.

The coastguard said it had rescued 18 people, all of whom were Sudanese nationals. Four of the survivors were taken to hospital, including a toddler.

Authorities said it was not immediately clear what caused the deaths, but they believe the boat had been at sea for days and had struggled to reach shore due to strong winds.

Crete remains one of several key gateways for migrants attempting to reach Europe from the Middle East and North Africa, with more than 22,000 of the 86,400 sea arrivals so far this year landing in Crete alone.

One unnamed coastguard official who spoke to news agency Reuters on condition of anonymity said the survivors were "shivering from the cold".

The migrants' boat was spotted by a Moroccan-flagged container ship about 15 nautical miles (28km) off Crete's coast.

The Greek coastguard rescued another 187 people in three separate incidents off the coast of Greece on Monday.

More than 37,000 migrants have arrived in Greece so far this year, UN figures show, already surpassing the number who arrived in the entirety of 2025.

Huang has acknowledged he had been intimate with a business executive, issuing an apology to his wife and to the company in an open letter posted on Nvidia's website. He did not name the woman.

Nvidia is opening an investigation into reports that CEO Jensen Huang was the "target of a foreign intelligence effort," the company's board of directors said Sunday.

The announcement came after Huang acknowledged to the board that he had been intimate with a business executive whom, according to The New York Times, U.S. intelligence determined was gathering information for Beijing.

In a letter to Nvidia employees obtained by The Associated Press, Huang said he had been unfaithful to his wife and apologized to his family and colleagues. He said he took "full responsibility" for his actions.

Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News

"Leading Nvidia is the privilege of my life," Huang wrote. "My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility."

Nvidia's board said it has "no reason to believe" that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, but that its inquiry would examine all available information. Huang "fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it," the board said.

"Today's news will not slow Nvidia," company spokesperson John Rizzo said in a statement. "Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as CEO without interruption."

Nvidia has become a central player in the global race to develop artificial intelligence, with its chips powering many of the data centers and computing systems used to train and run AI models. Its advanced processors have also been a focus of U.S. export restrictions aimed at limiting China's access to cutting-edge semiconductor technology.

national.title: Krakow shooting suspect has died in hospital, police say
national.summary: Six people were killed in the shooting, and three bodies of the suspect's family members were found at their home.
national.body:
A gunman suspected of killing six people in central Krakow, and his parents and sister at their home, died in hospital early on Monday, Polish police have said.

The 24-year-old, who has been named as Michal Oksinski by local media, was injured after opening fire in central Krakow, the second largest city in Poland, on Saturday, police said.

Armed officers raced to the scene and engaged in a gunfight with the suspect, who was shot within three minutes of the attack beginning, preventing a further massacre, officials said.

Officials initially reported the gunman had apparently been inspired by "far-right ideologies", but have since said they are still investigating any possible motivation.

After the shooting, which began shortly before 15:00 local time (14:00 GMT) in Krakow's busy Main Market Square, police identified the attacker as a 24-year-old Polish man.

In the hours after the shooting, a minister said early investigations indicate he was inspired by "far-right ideologies". The minister also described him as an "ultra-nationalist" without giving further details.

However, during a press briefing on Monday morning, Przemysław Nowak, a spokesperson for Poland's National Prosecutor's Office, said investigations into his motive remain ongoing.

Six people - four women and two men - are confirmed to have been killed in the attack.

A Dunkirk resident is facing charges after an investigation into narcotics activity ended with a search warrant being executed last week.

Chautauqua County Sheriff’s Narcotics Investigators had observed Germaine Dias, 49, walking in the area of 515 Main St. in the city. Dias was detained at this location by narcotics investigators due to the search warrant. As a result of the search, investigators seized 28.18 grams of crack cocaine, 5.15 grams of fentanyl, 3.95 grams of cocaine, 74 dosage units of suboxone, scales and packaging material used for the sale and distribution of narcotics and $1,653.

Dias was charged with two counts of third-degree criminal possession of a controlled substance, seventh-degree criminal possession of a controlled substance and second-degree criminally using drug paraphernalia.

Dias was transported to the City of Dunkirk Police Department and was to be arraigned in the Dunkirk City Court. Officers from Dunkirk Police Department and Detectives from Jamestown Police Department assisted on this investigation.

local.title: National Comedy Center launches caregiver week honoring New York couple
local.summary: The National Comedy Center will offer complimentary admission to caregivers and the loved ones they care for during its first Susan Sargent Caregiver Week, running November 9 through November 15.

It honors the memory of Susan Sargent and was inspired by her visit to the museum with her husband and caregiver, Mitch Goldman.Susan had frontotemporal dementia, a condition that affected her ability to communicate and connect. Goldman became her full-time caregiver."Susan had become largely nonverbal, and in order to connect at night as a married couple, they would watch comedy," said Journey Gunderson, the Comedy Center's executive director. "They found that if they could laugh together at the same punch lines, they could still feel that connection."During their visit to the museum, classic comedy and interactive exhibits prompted memories and speech."She really connected there. She got her memory back and speech back for a short time, and it was wonderful," he added. That experience became a foundation for the Comedy Center's Comedy & Caregiving initiative. Contributions made in Susan's memory are funding the new week."Visiting the National Comedy Center was an extraordinary experience for Susan and me," Goldman said in a statement. "At a time when conversation had become difficult, laughing together brought back memories and gave us a way to connect. local.title: New York's first confirmed case of chronic wasting disease in 21 years is found in a Livingston County deer
local.summary: The highly contagious illness is always fatal to deer, but there is no evidence it can be transmitted to humans.
local.body:
The New York state Department of Environmental Conservation has confirmed that a wild deer killed by a hunter in the Livingston County town of Sparta had chronic wasting disease.

This is the first time in over 20 years the highly contagious and fatal disease has been detected in New York.

The state's last outbreak in 2005 was contained following a testing and culling operation.

The untreatable illness, which spreads among deer and elk, is caused by misfolded proteins called prions that affect an animal’s brain and nervous system.

While there is no evidence that chronic wasting disease can be contracted by humans or domestic animals, the CDC advises NOT eating venison from any deer known to be infected.

The DEC has established a geographic containment area around the towns of Conesus, Groveland, North Dansville, Sparta, Springwater and West Sparta.

Hunters there must submit tissue samples from their harvested deer to the agency. And deer may not be transported outside the containment zone.

The DEC will be hosting a virtual information session on Nov. 17 at 7 p.m.

local.title: NY Gov. Hochul won with a mandate from voters. But what was the message?
local.summary: The nationwide blue wave was seen as a repudiation of President Trump.
local.body:
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul scored the type of political victory on Election Day that typically comes with a mandate — but what message voters were trying to send depends on who you ask.

The Democratic governor topped her Republican opponent Bruce Blakeman by about 20 percentage points, or 1.2 million votes, tripling her margin of victory from the last time she ran in 2022. She increased her vote share in every single one of New York’s 62 counties, in red and blue areas alike, and won eight counties she lost four years ago — including Nassau, where Blakeman is county executive.

But what, exactly, does that result tell us about what voters are expecting from Hochul in her second full term? Everyone seems to have a different answer.

Christina Greer, a Fordham University political science professor, said the blue wave that swept the nation on Election Day — which saw Democrats win key races in traditionally Republican states — makes a New York-specific mandate difficult to define.

“I'm not sure if the governor has a mandate, and I think this goes for not just Kathy Hochul, but a lot of the Democrats who were successful on Tuesday,” she said. “I think we need to be careful as to: Is it a vote for Kathy Hochul, or is it a vote against Donald Trump?”

Hochul’s campaign also focused on tying Blakeman to Trump, his friend and ally who headlined a rally in Syracuse just before voters started casting their ballots. Her ads frequently included a clip of Blakeman saying he would “never be disloyal” to the Republican president.

More than 60% of voters in New York view the president unfavorably, according to recent public opinion polls . Many voters blamed Trump for raising the price of gas through the war in Iran.

“ The Democrat message last night was basically, ’We’re not him,’” said Republican political consultant Mike Dawidziak. “And that message worked last night, but it’s not gonna work in two years.”

local.body:
NEW ORLEANS (AP) -- Saints second-year quarterback Tyler Shough likes to think he has a refined and thoughtful approach to remaining calm and in control in the clutch.

He backed it up against the Cleveland Browns and fellow second-year QB Shedeur Sanders on Sunday.

Shough floated a 15-yard timing pass to Juwan Johnson toward the right corner of the end zone for a touchdown for New Orleans in overtime, and the desperate Saints stopped a do-or-die, 2-point conversion to hold on, 23-22.

“We go down to the end of the game, he gets better and better,” Saints receiver Chris Olave said of Shough. “He’s calm and collected and we’ve got the utmost confidence in Tyler.”

After the Saints (3-5) scored on the first possession of overtime, Cleveland answered when Harold Fannin Jr. turned a short pass from Sanders into a tackle-breaking, 39-yard touchdown with a minute left in overtime.

The Browns (5-4) opted for a 2-point conversion for the win, but Sanders was forced to roll right under pressure from Carl Granderson and threw incomplete, giving the Saints their first win at home this season.

“We looked at ourself in the mirror and we know what we’ve got to do,” said Granderson, who had two of the Saints’ five sacks. “It’s time to turn this thing around now and we’re excited to get the next one. So, stay tuned.”

Cleveland coach Todd Monken said he never considered kicking the extra point.

CORTLAND -- The historic postseason run of the Fredonia State women’s soccer team came to an end on Saturday as the Blue Devils fell to Cortland 4-1 in the SUNYAC Tournament final at Holloway Field.

The appearance marked the first trip to the conference championship game in program history for Fredonia, which concluded one of the most successful seasons the program has ever enjoyed with a 12-4-4 record. The 12 wins matched a school record previously reached by the 2011, 2012 and 2024 teams.

Gabby Irwin had the lone Devil goal, converting a penalty kick during the 89th minute. Goalkeeper Alyssa Hatch totaled 10 saves. Hatch, Irwin and Makayla Stainbrook were selected to the SUNYAC All-Tournament Team.

Cortland struck first in the 13th minute when Gianna Cirilla headed home a free kick service for a 1-0 lead. The Red Dragons doubled the advantage less than five minutes later as Tyla Vuotto redirected a cross into the net, and Leah Rehm extended the lead to 3-0 with a long-range strike in the 43rd minute.

Cirilla added her second goal of the match in the 87th minute to make it 4-0 before Fredonia answered in the closing moments. After a foul in the penalty area, Irwin converted her PK after she was taken down in the box.

BUFFALO (AP) -- Tomas Hertl scored two goals and the Vegas Golden Knights won their third straight game, 4-1 over the Buffalo Sabres on Sunday.

Hertl scored both of his goals in the third period to help put the game away for the Golden Knights, who finished their road trip 3-0-1.

Jack Eichel and Mitch Marner also scored for Vegas while Adin Hill made 27 saves.

Beck Malenstyn scored and Colten Ellis made 21 saves for Buffalo, which has lost two of its last three games.

Marner opened the scoring with a short-handed goal at 12:17 of the second period following a turnover by Tage Thompson.

Eichel, who was the Sabres first-round draft pick in 2015 and traded to Vegas in 2021, made it 2-0 one minute and 26 seconds later with his eighth goal of the season. He has seven goals and three assists in eight games against Buffalo in his career.

Malenstyn cut the Vegas lead to 2-1 with his first goal on a goalmouth scrum at 4:26 of the third period, but Hertl made it 3-1 just 1:17 later.

Hertl’s second of the game and ninth of the season made it 4-1 at 10:00.

local.body:
MADRID (AP) -- Joe Burrow threw for three touchdowns and rushed for another and the Cincinnati Bengals’ offense kept rolling to defeat the Atlanta Falcons 34-17 in Madrid on Sunday for their fourth straight win.

Ja’Marr Chase had eight receptions for 142 yards in the first half, and Tee Higgins added two touchdown catches at Real Madrid’s Santiago Bernabeu Stadium. Chase finished with 10 catches for 155 yards and a touchdown.

After his 47-yard touchdown catch in the first quarter, Chase celebrated with Higgins in bullfighting style, with Higgins mimicking a bull by putting his hands on his head and Chase playing the matador with an imaginary cape.

The Bengals (6-2) have scored 30 points or more in four straight games for the first time since 1997. It was the second consecutive defeat for the Falcons (3-6).

Burrow, who completed 24 of 29 passes for 271 yards Sunday, had thrown five touchdown passes and rushed for another in overtime in the team’s 43-36 win over the Tennessee Titans last week.

MIAMI GARDENS, Fla. (AP) -- Jahmyr Gibbs had a rushing touchdown, Jared Goff threw for 170 yards and Detroit beat Miami for its fourth straight victory.

Jake Bates made four field goals on a day that was a bit underwhelming for Goff and the Lions’ top-ranked offense, which entered averaging 29 points and 395.4 yards per game but finished with 271 yards.

Goff completed 17 of 25 passes while being sacked three times as Miami’s defense pressured him throughout. Goff was intercepted by rookie cornerback Chris Johnson on a tipped pass in the first quarter -- just the second pick he has thrown this season.

local.summary: Bob Winner, the former legendary Clymer Central School boys basketball coach, was laid to rest last Friday morning at a graveside service in Corry, Pennsylvania. He was 90 years old. Dennis Hinsdale, one of Winner’s former players, needed only two words and two syllables to describe his longtime fri
local.body:
OBSERVER File Photo In this February 1993 file photo, Bob Winner holds aloft a commemorative basketball in recognition of his 400th career victory as the boys varsity coach at Clymer Central School.

OBSERVER File Photo In this March 1993 file photo, Clymer boys varsity basketball coach Bob Winner is seen during the Section VI Class D championship game at the University at Buffalo’s Alumni Arena. The Pirates defeated Ripley for the title, 60-53.

Bob Winner, the former legendary Clymer Central School boys basketball coach, was laid to rest last Friday morning at a graveside service in Corry, Pennsylvania. He was 90 years old. Dennis Hinsdale, one of Winner's former players, needed only two words and two syllables to describe his longtime friend: "The best."

"He taught us more about life than just playing basketball," said Hinsdale (Class of 1973).

No one can argue that point, because Winner's influence was felt in all circumstances, not just on game nights.

"I had graduated and he was still the athletic director," Hinsdale recalled. "I said to him, 'Hey, if you ever need a coach, I'd be interested.' He said that he would keep that in mind. ... A year later, he called me and asked if I was still interested because he had an opening."

Years later, Hinsdale coached the Lady Pirates to the 2009-2010 New York State Public High School Athletic Association title.

During his tenure at Clymer, Winner guided the program to seven league championships; four Section VI titles; and posted an overall record of 407-267. His 1972-73 team, which claimed league and sectional crowns, was unbeaten, finishing 20-0.

Business Manager Josh Melquist reported that the change orders for the Capital Improvement Project total around $144,000. “This is still well under what was planned for,” he said.

The board approved a Capital Improvement contract with Landscape Structures, Inc. for a new playground. Board member Tom Tarpley said he was disappointed to see that the district would be charged more than a half million dollars. “I feel that the district is being overcharged and taken advantage of,” he said. “I will vote to approve the contract since the project has been voter approved, but the district needs to find a better way in the future to prevent us being unfairly charged.”

Sikorski also told board members that current ex-officio student board members, Liberty Maring and Grace Wolfe accompanied him to the student ex-officio conference at BOCES. “They were able to network with other ex-officio student board members from Southwestern, Maple Grove and Cassadaga Valley about their positions to learn more about what they are doing while serving as ex-officio members,” he said.

Also in his report, Sikorski told the board that the state Education Department is planning to de-couple the Regents exams from the graduation requirements. Beginning in January 2028, there will only be one diploma issued. The freshman class of 2028 will be the first to experience this, he said.

entertainment.title: Kevin Costner’s new fragrance reminds him of ‘carpets and wood and guns’
entertainment.summary: The "Yellowstone" star teamed up with 19-69 on a trio of scents — one of which is like catnip for pregnant women, apparently.
entertainment.body:
Great news for anyone who’s ever wanted to smell like Kevin Costner: The “Yellowstone” star is now a perfumer, having developed a trio of scents with Milan-based fragrance house 19-69 .

Costner discovered the company almost a decade ago, when he used — and promptly became infatuated with — its Rainbow Bar body wash during a hotel stay in Germany.

The 71-year-old Oscar winner tracked down not only a case of the product for his own home, but also the contact info for the brand’s co-founder, Johan Bergelin.

Over the course of the following two years, Bergelin and Costner collaborated on After Hours , Pacific Coast Highway and Heritage . Available now, they’ll set you back $80 for a 0.25-ounce bottle, $300 for 1.01 ounces, or — if you’re really smitten — $800 for 3.21 ounces.

The cypress, bourbon and nutmeg blend After Hours is the signature scent of the collection, with Bergelin telling GQ that it “evokes the image of someone in a glass house in the Hollywood Hills at sunset, surveying the city.”

Costner paints an even more vivid image, bringing it back to his May 1989 cover of Vanity Fair , shot by Helmut Newton.

“So, I was in a tuxedo but my tie was off and my jacket was on the couch,” he told GQ. “It was supposed to be a sexy shot with a glass of whiskey. And Helmut kept saying, ‘take your shirt off, just leave the bow tie on or something’… I said no. I’m not an exotic dancer!”

Apparently, After Hours is also like catnip for expectant mothers; Costner told the outlet that while field-testing the fragrance during one of his son’s volleyball games, a pregnant woman approached him with an inquiry.
